messages.subject: Warning message ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
messages.subject_clean: Warning message ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
messages.body_plain:
Dear Eric et al

I am a Distance sampling beginner, and am trying to run a basic CDS analysis on a set of survey data without post-stratification. I have 6 study sites surveyed using point counts with 10 points per site repeated three times each. The size of the study sites vary and I have put this variable in a column entitled 'Block size'. There are 662 observations, each of single dogs (i.e. no clusters). I followed the instructions in the Distance 7.3 user guide page 25 under the section Example 2: More Complex Data Import. My data follow an identical structure to the example given - House Wren, with the one difference that only one observer collected data (hence I did not post-stratify). The analysis runs but the output gives me the error message ' Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity' and has an orange ball instead of a green one when the analysis is computed. I assume this means the reliability of the output is compromised? I actually only need to calculate a strip width in order to retrospectively truncate my data (I am not particularly interested in number of dogs per se but more detectability over specified distances in the day versus the night).

Are you able to a) confirm that I do need to reanalyse my data (i.e. can't ignore the error message!) or b) advise as to what might be the problem.

Many thanks in advance,

Bryony

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Warning message ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Warning message ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
messages.body_plain:
Bryony

Welcome to the list.

Your interpretation of the warning message is approximately correct.  The software is confronted with two conflicting instructions: fit the data the best you can and ensure the function you fit to the data such that the fitted detection function is at its highest at distance 0 does not increase anywhere as a function of increasing distance.

The message arises because Distance cannot do both.  Often this arises because the histogram of observed distances tails off at large distances, but there may be a couple of detections at very large distances.  The software would like to fit a function that declines, but then increases to fit the pod of distant detections.

The customary way of getting rid of the warning is, as you would guess, truncate the data to exclude those most distant detections; they usually carry little information about the shape of the detection function in the region where shape of the function is most critical.

I hope that answers your question about the warning message.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,

In one sense, it's fine to use p-values to do this selection.

However, if your parametric terms vary in space then you may have
problems. As illustrated in this paper,

https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~bjreich/papers/FixedEffectsYouLove.pdf

when you include a spatial random effect (e.g., a smooth of space) to
your model, you can change the effect size of parametric terms in the
model. In this case your p-values will not be "correct". This may be
especially problematic if you intend to interpret those effect sizes.
Selection via AIC or other statistics won't get around this issue. This
is somewhat of an open problem in spatial statistics, most recently
addressed in this (somewhat technical in places) paper:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.09420

If you don't intend to interpret the effect size (and only intend to
estimate abundance) or if your fixed effects don't vary in space then
this is less of an issue and using, say, p-values will likely be okay.

Hope this helps.

--dave

messages.subject: Comparison between DS and DSM estimates from same dataset
messages.subject_clean: Comparison between DS and DSM estimates from same dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am interested in comparing the abundance estimates calculated by both distance sampling and density surface modelling approaches.

Indeed, I estimated population abundance for several species using both methods, and I am currently wondering to what extent the abundance estimates can be different. Firstly, I would have expected estimates to be reasonably similar, but because dsm models add ecological information, I am considering that it may be acceptable that estimates drawn by each method could differ, although it remains to be determined to what extent these estimates could differ.

Here are some precisions about the methods I used.

The study area was divided into 4 regions, and I wished to estimate abundance in only one of these regions. As a first step, I ran distance sampling analyses on my entire count data for a given species, selected a probability of detection for this species, and estimated the size of its population in the region of interest using the function dht2 and a geographical stratification.

As a second step, I ran density surface models on the same species using a subset of the count data corresponding to the region of interest (i.e. the region where I specifically wished to measure population abundance), and, after selecting the best model for that species, I calculated its abundance in the area using the predict function.

Then, I compared the estimates that I obtained for the region of interest using both dht2 and predict functions. These estimates get more or less close to each other depending on the species studied (in rare cases, the estimate obtained with the dsm analysis (ex. ~47250 individuals) was equal to more than twice the estimate obtained with the ds analysis (ex. 23034 individuals)).

I could not find any information in the literature mentioning what gap between the two measures could be acceptable, and therefore, I wish to discuss with you about the comparison of these two methods for the same dataset.

Would anyone have any opinion or any reading to share on this matter? To what extent do you think the estimates calculated from the two methods could differ? I would be really interested to hear what you think of this!

Many thanks in advance!

Delphine

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Comparison between DS and DSM estimates from same dataset
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Comparison between DS and DSM estimates from same dataset
messages.body_plain:
Delphine

Both methods should estimate a similar number of animals in the covered region (region within distance "w" of the transect).  Conventional distance sampling extrapolates to the remainder of the area based upon the design (placement of transects) being representative of the entire area.  Density surface models are based upon models to make inference to the portions of the study area that did not receive effort.  In the situation where both the design is good and the model is good, they may produce similar estimates.

You can think of reasons why design-based extrapolation may not be a good idea (non-representative locations sampled) and likewise reasons why model-based inference may be poor (uncommon combinations of explanatory covariates occur infrequently in the covered area, but more frequently in the non-covered area).  There is no a priori expectation regarding the agreement of the two methods of inference.

The other element missing from your explanation is the amount of uncertainty associated with each estimate.  The point estimates may differ markedly, yet if they possess high amounts of uncertainty, inference from the estimates may not differ radically.

> Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,
>
> In one sense, it's fine to use p-values to do this selection.
>
> However, if your parametric terms vary in space then you may have
> problems. As illustrated in this paper,
>
> https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~bjreich/papers/FixedEffectsYouLove.pdf
>
> when you include a spatial random effect (e.g., a smooth of space) to
> your model, you can change the effect size of parametric terms in the
> model. In this case your p-values will not be "correct". This may be
> especially problematic if you intend to interpret those effect sizes.
> Selection via AIC or other statistics won't get around this issue. This
> is somewhat of an open problem in spatial statistics, most recently
> addressed in this (somewhat technical in places) paper:
> https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.09420
>
> If you don't intend to interpret the effect size (and only intend to
> estimate abundance) or if your fixed effects don't vary in space then
> this is less of an issue and using, say, p-values will likely be okay.

> Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Model choice, AIC, Goodness of fit, and DSsim
messages.subject_clean: Model choice, AIC, Goodness of fit, and DSsim
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm looking to bounce some questions off of the group mostly about model selection.

I completed a line-transect aerial helicopter distance sampling survey of wild sheep, flying a systematic, parallel transect design that had a randomized starting point.  Transects were spaced 1000 m apart.  The results were encouraging, with > 70 group sightings of sheep.  For the analysis, I had to bin distances in 50 m bins because I believe there is uncertainty for each distance measurement.   I have done some analysis and wondered if anyone could provide some input.

I completed an AIC analysis of half normal, hazard rate, and uniform detection functions.  Half normal was the best model and showed no evidence for lack of fit, with a p-value of .8 for the goodness of fit test.  Then I added size (sheep group size) as a covariate to the half normal detection function and ran another AIC for those two models. The results show that the model with size for covariate beat the null model by ~ 130.  That is great except for when I run a goodness of fit test for the covariate model, the p-value returned was .053, just barely failing to reject.  Also, the plot of the detection function nor the q-q plot (see attached) are not all that convincing.

I wonder your thoughts for model choice here?

I was also wondering if the DSsim package might at all be useful in this context to run diagnostics on my survey design.

Thanks,

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Model choice, AIC, Goodness of fit, and DSsim
messages.body_plain:
Leo

Some off-the-cuff comments about your analyses, based upon your description and figures.
Regarding goodness of fit; I don't place much weight in the size of the GOF p-value.  Anything over 0.05 (or your favourite alpha value) is adequate.
Looking at your second detection function figure, it would seem that the majority of your sightings were of "large" groups.  The modelling suggests those groups have perfect detectability our to your truncation distance (450m?).
you have only a few detections of non-large groups.  I speculate the two points in the 100-150m bin with detection probabilities estimated between 0.2 and 0.35 are of singletons.
there's a second trail of detections of perhaps 5 groups, where group size is probably pairs, then a few more detections around 300m perhaps of groups of size 3?
I'm guessing maybe 10 of the 70 detections are of non-large groups, the remainder of the detections being of groups sufficiently large that detectability is estimated to be perfect out to the truncation distance.

In summary, your design is such that the covered areas for adjacent transects abut one another; you are covering essentially 100% of your study area; lucky to have the resources to do that.  By placing the transects in that proximity, detectability of the majority of animals in the population (in groups) does not diminish perceptibly (as best I can judge by interpreting your figures).  I'm not sure what else a simulation might tell you.

I'm not inclined to suggest any alterations to your analysis.  If there were a greater number of detections of non-large groups, I might suggest treating the large groups as a strip transect (estimating abundance of individuals in big groups), then fitting detection function models to the non-large groups and producing a second abundance estimate of this remainder of the population.  However, with only ~10 detections of the small groups, you'll not produce defensible detection functions.

messages.body_plain:
Darren

Thanks for your question, this is the right place to raise it.

Your diagnosis that "ddf.3" is the cause of the error you received when trying to fit the dsm model "x+y".  The remedy however is not to have "ddf.3" shipped with the software, but rather to have that object preserved after it has been created by analysis 3 ("detection fn - Hazard rate").

Conducting analysis 5 (dsm x+y) is dependent upon the existence of the result produced in analysis 3 (ddf.3).  The Distance for Windows software will tidy after itself, by removing R objects created in previous analysis steps, unless you request that those objects not be tidied.

The solution is to open the Distance Preferences Window, the R Options tab (seen below).  Make sure neither of the two boxes circled are ticked.  This will preserve previous R objects (such as "ddf.3") so they are available in subsequent analysis steps.

Let us know if this solves your problem.

messages.subject_clean: Source code of MCDS.exe (the one under Distance 7.3 software) ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello.

As already explained last year, I'm currently developing a python library to make it simpler and safer to run numerous CDS analyses (Distance is great, but not that easy when you want to run numerous identical analyses (same parameters, at least tens) on multiple samples (tens or hundreds)), while keeping at the same time manual access to all the analyses results and especially output curves for keeping an eye on what's happening (statistically and "birdly" speaking).

Of course, this library is based on calls of the MCDS executable shipped with Distance 7.3 (the file has this timestamp : 2014-03-27, and it is version 6.2.0 according to the log files).

It works great under windows (7, 10) but I'd like to port it to NATIVE Linux (avoiding virtualisation software for obvious simplicity and performances reasons).

So ... would it be possible to get access to MCDS 6.2 source code in order to compile it under Linux ?

Of course, I would give you back any script or makefile that I would build for that (my work has no commercial purpose at all, only for "science", in my free time, for a small cummunity of French Massif Central birders).
And I would also strictly follow your instructions, whatever they are, about how this source code, or else MCDS linux binary, could be shared (or not) with my fellow birders and "distance samplers".

Thanks in advance for your help.

Jean-Philippe MEURET
(long time professional developer and data analyst, free time birder and "distance sampler" in Clermont-Ferrand, France).

PS: I know that older versions of MCDS have been released as source code ... but they are too old :-)

Hi Hypolais and list,

We're very open to making the source code public again, and will do so
when time allows. Meantime I'm happy to send it to anyone who asks.  It
is written mostly in FORTRAN 77 with a small piece of FORTRAN 90.
However, you should be aware of one fundamental limitation in using it:
compiling it requires a commercial numerical library (the IMSL Fortran
Library) -- we have permission to distribute the software for free with
the routine we use from this library compiled in, but not to distribute
the library itself.

Given the above, it one possibly simpler options would be for you to
call the Distance or mrds packages in R from Python (I believe the
Python package rpy2  https://rpy2.github.io/ enables this).  Even
simpler would be to work in R rather than Python ;)

I'm happy to correspond further with you off-list, and we can post back
to the list whatever solution we come up with.

Best wishes, Len Thomas
